involving 1,3-enynes and iodides was systematically inves-
tigated under the optimized conditions (Scheme 2). Enyne

Scheme 2. Substrate Scope Investigation
To further broaden the scope of this methodology, we
explored the applicability of iodides bearing diverse sub-
stituents and substitution patterns. Evaluation of the substrate
scope revealed excellent compatibility with aryl iodides
containing neutral (methyl, isopropyl, phenyl), electron-
donating (methoxy, phenoxy), and electron-withdrawing
(chloro, cyano, boronate ester, trifluoromethoxy, trifluoro-
methyl, ester) groups (18−28, 47%−80%). Nevertheless,
strongly electron-withdrawing substituents led to markedly
diminished reaction eficiency, as reflected in substantially
lower yields (24, 27). Aryl iodides with ortho or meta
substituents and disubstituted aryl iodides both maintained
good yields (29−31), indicating high tolerance to steric
hindrance. Fused-ring iodides (32), sulfur-containing hetero-
cyclic iodides (33), and nitrogen- containing heterocyclic
iodides (34) all aforded moderate yields, demonstrating good
heteroatom compatibility. In addition to aryl iodides, the
methodology was successfully extended to alkyl iodides, as
exemplified by the eficient conversion of secondary
iodocyclohexane (35), N-Boc-4-iodopiperidine (36), and
tertiaryiodoadamantane (37). In contrast, primary alkyl halides
exhibited limited reactivity under the current conditions. The
method exhibited excellent applicability for the late-stage
modification of complex molecules, as iodinated derivatives of
L- Menthol, Nerol, Empagliflozin intermediate, and Alectinib
intermediate all provided the target carboxylated products in
moderate yields (38−41), highlighting its utility for the late-
stage functionalization of bioactive molecules.
